titleStmt.title: Duplication Based Integrated Task and Message Scheduling on a Heterogeneous Network of Workstations (NOWs)

analytic.title: Duplication Based Integrated Task and Message Scheduling on a Heterogeneous Network of Workstations (NOWs)

div.p: This paper proposes a duplication based algorithm called Integrated Duplication based Scheduling Algorithm (InDuSA) capable of scheduling hard and soft real-time tasks and messages on precedence related NOWs. The system is heterogeneous in that a task can have diverse execution times on different workstations. Given a mix of hard and soft real-time tasks, our algorithm assigns higher priority to hard tasks. Once the tasks are scheduled, the proposed scheme duplicates certain tasks. Doing so reduces the inter-processor communication time between communicating tasks assigned to different workstations. This enables certain tasks to start (and finish) earlier. Hence, the schedulability increases. Moreover, the proposed scheme is scalable in that it can generate a schedule even if a sufficient number of processors are not available. Initial simulation results suggest that the proposed scheme offers better schedulability as compared to other algorithms in the literature when there is significant communication in the system.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: A real-time system is defined as one that is required to complete its work and deliver its services on a timely basis [1]. Based on the "seriousness" of deadline misses, real-time systems can be classified into two types -hard real-time systems and soft realtime systems. In the former, it is absolutely essential that all tasks deadlines are met, else the consequences could be catastrophic. An example of a hard real-time system is the braking system of an automobile. When the driver presses the brake, the system needs to respond appropriately else the automobile can meet with an accident. On the other hand, some laxity of task deadlines is tolerated in soft real-time examples. Consider an on-line transaction system. The user does not mind is there is a little delay in the processing of his/her transaction, as long as it is within "acceptable" limits.

div.head: Proposed scheme
div.p: In this section, the working of the proposed scheme InDuSa is explained. The pseudocode of the proposed scheme is shown in Figure 1. a real-time task (hard or soft). For each DAG, the nodes represent the real-time tasks and the edges between them represent the precedence relationship between the tasks [4]. The tasks are precedence related in that a task cannot start execution till it receives the computation results from all of its predecessor tasks. Since a task can have potentially different execution times on different processors, its execution requirement is represented in the form of an execution time array.

The set of processors are connected by a point-topoint network. A deadline driven protocol called the earliest-due-date-deadline (EDD-D) is used to schedule messages between the real-time subtasks [5]. When a subtask called the sender s wishes to send a message to subtask called the destination d, EDD-D sets up an s d channel. The set of messages in the system is given by M = {m 1 , m 2 , m 3 … m n }. Each message is characterized by its deadline, which is given by d(m i ), given that m i ∈ M. Messages are scheduled to be transmitted on links between processor pairs. Each link can be represented as l d ∈L, where L is the set of links.

div.head: Initial simulation results
div.p: The proposed scheme InDuSa has been compared with relevant algorithms from the literature, namely RTPSA [2] and AEAP [6]. The first measure is the Success Ratio (SR), which is the number of task sets that meet their deadlines to the total number of tasks. The total communication to total computation ratio (CCR) is defined as (total edge cost/ (total node cost). The CCR value is a measure of the amount of communication in the system.

Figure 2 shows the effect of Message Load (= number of messages/number of tasks in the application) on the Success ratio of the application (with CCR = 1.0, number of tasks = 200 (100 hard and 100 soft tasks)). It can be seen that as the message load increases, the success ratio experiences a decrement. This can be explained as follows. A larger message load implies more messages that need to be scheduled in the system (for the same task load). This translates to a higher load on the channels and consequently, tasks start (and finish) later. Hence, the success ratio drops. However, it can be seen that the proposed scheme InDuSa offers better SR values as compared to the other schemes. That is because task duplication reduces the IPC time between tasks assigned to different processors. Hence, more tasks start (and finish) earlier. This translates to a better success ratio for InDuSa. We also plan to study the effect of schedulability on scalability, hard and soft load, communication and heterogeneity.
